data.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
data.summary:
Input: A list of intervals where each interval is [start, end].
Output: The minimum number of intervals to remove to make the remaining intervals non-overlapping.
Rules: Intervals that touch at the endpoints are not considered overlapping.

steps.title: Handle edge cases
steps.detail: If the intervals list is empty, return 0 removals needed.

steps.title: Sort the intervals
steps.detail: Sort the intervals based on their end times in ascending order.

steps.title: Greedy selection
steps.detail: Iterate through the sorted intervals. Keep track of the end time of the last accepted interval. If the current interval starts before the last accepted interval ends, it overlaps and must be removed. Otherwise, accept it and update the last end time.

data.space_complexity: O(log n) or O(n) depending on the sorting algorithm implementation.

data.pattern_summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step with the hope of finding the global optimum. Reach for this pattern when asked to optimize a resource allocation or find a maximum/minimum set of non-conflicting items.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Making a locally optimal choice, such as picking the interval that ends earliest, leads to the global maximum of non-overlapping intervals.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While you could use DP by sorting and checking subproblems, a greedy strategy is more efficient and simpler here since making the earliest-ending choice is always globally safe.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually work on sorted arrays with a linear scan maintaining a sliding window or converging bounds, whereas we need to evaluate selection choices across multiple intervals.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps are used for O(1) frequency counting or existence checks, which does not help resolve scheduling conflicts between overlapping ranges.

signals.phrase: minimum number of intervals to remove
signals.hint: Minimizing removals is equivalent to maximizing the count of intervals you can keep.
Implies you must track and compare the boundaries of adjacent items to detect conflicts.

data.brute_force_idea: Generate every possible subset of intervals using bitmasking, check each subset to see if its intervals overlap, and find the size of the largest valid subset. Subtract that size from the total number of intervals to get the minimum removals.
data.brute_force_why: There are 2^n possible subsets. For each subset, we generate it in O(n) time, sort it, and check all adjacent pairs for overlap, which adds extra overhead.
data.bottleneck: Iterating through every possible subset of intervals takes exponential time, which becomes impossible to compute as n grows large.
bottleneck_hints: Consider how many total combinations of intervals exist for a list of size n.
Notice that checking every combination requires generating 2^n subsets.
Ask yourself if you need to test every subset or if you can make a smart local choice at each step instead.

data.overview: The algorithm finds the minimum number of intervals to remove by sorting them based on their end times and greedily keeping the ones that finish earliest. This leaves the maximum room for remaining intervals, minimizing overlaps.
data.intuition: Imagine scheduling meetings in a single room. To fit as many meetings as possible, always choose the meeting that ends the earliest so you have the maximum time left for future meetings.

pitfalls: Sorting by start time instead of end time, which fails the greedy choice property.
Forgetting that touching endpoints (e.g., [1,2] and [2,3]) do not count as overlapping.
Failing to handle empty interval lists correctly.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach checks every possible subset of intervals, leading to exponential time. The optimized approach removes this bottleneck by sorting the intervals by their end times and iterating through them once using a greedy strategy. By always picking the interval that finishes earliest, we leave the maximum possible room for subsequent intervals.

derivation.note: Sorting the intervals by end time dominates the total time complexity.
The loop iterates through each remaining interval once.
Compares the current start time with the last kept end time.

data.time_summary: Line 6 takes O(n log n) for sorting. The loop from line 11 to 16 runs in O(n) linear time because it visits each interval once. Combining them yields O(n log n) total time, which matches the measured scaling behavior.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) or O(log n) depending on the Python sorting implementation used for the input list, plus a few scalar variables that take O(1) space.
data.takeaway: When dealing with interval scheduling or overlap problems, always sort by end time first to enable a greedy choice that maximizes remaining space.
mistakes: Sorting by start time instead of end time, which fails to greedily leave the maximum room for future intervals.
Forgetting that intervals touching at endpoints are not considered overlapping, which changes the strictness of the inequality check.
Attempting to solve subset generation with exponential brute force instead of recognizing the greedy substructure.
